article.description: El hielo cerca de la cumbre del pico montañoso indonesio se ha reducido a parches dispersos demasiado pequeños para fluir como glaciares.
article.explanation:
**El último hielo en el Puncak Jaya**

El Puncak Jaya, ubicado en la cordillera Sudirman de Indonesia, ha sido uno de los pocos lugares cerca del ecuador donde el hielo ha persistido durante todo el año. Sin embargo, las imágenes satelitales muestran una alarmante reducción de sus glaciares. En 1988, estos cubrían aproximadamente 4.31 kilómetros cuadrados, mientras que para septiembre de 2025, solo quedaban alrededor de 0.09 kilómetros cuadrados, lo que representa cerca del 2% de su extensión original.

El espesor del hielo también ha disminuido drásticamente. En 2010, el hielo en el sitio de monitoreo principal tenía una altura de 32 metros, pero para 2023, este se redujo a solo 4 metros. Este proceso de adelgazamiento ha llevado a que los glaciares se fragmenten, creando bordes expuestos que aceleran el derretimiento.

Los científicos advierten que, debido a las condiciones climáticas actuales y fenómenos como El Niño, la desaparición total de estos glaciares podría ocurrir alrededor de 2030. Durante eventos de El Niño pasados, el hielo se ha derretido a un ritmo alarmante, lo que subraya la vulnerabilidad de estas masas de hielo en un clima cambiante.

Bare rock appears brown, and glacial ice, shown in blue, caps several of the highest ridges. Vegetation at lower elevations appears green. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A false-color satellite image shows the same area in 2026. Only a few small fragments of ice remain, shown in blue, and bare brown rock covers most of the ridgetops that were icy in 1988. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin 1988 2026 A false-color satellite image from 1988 shows mountain ridges of Indonesia’s Sudirman Range. Bare rock appears brown, and glacial ice, shown in blue, caps several of the highest ridges. Vegetation at lower elevations appears green. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A false-color satellite image shows the same area in 2026. Only a few small fragments of ice remain, shown in blue, and bare brown rock covers most of the ridgetops that were icy in 1988. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin 1988 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers. Positioned in the tropics beside the largest expanse of warm ocean water on Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round. Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “ canaries in the coal mine ,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, and the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania. The change on Puncak Jaya is visible in this image pair, acquired in 1988 by the TM (Thematic Mapper) on Landsat 5 (left) and in 2026 by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 (right). The false-color images help distinguish areas of ice (light blue) from exposed bedrock (brown). Clouds appear white and vegetation green. In 1988, the glaciers covered about 4.31 square kilometers (1.66 square miles), according to Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics ( BMKG ). By September 2025, satellite and aerial data showed that only about 0.09 square kilometers (0.03 square miles) remained—an area equivalent to about a dozen soccer fields. That’s roughly 2 percent of the 1988 extent . An aerial survey planned for December should yield an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, Permana said. The glaciers have thinned, too. Measurements at the primary monitoring site on the East Northwall Firn showed a drop from 32 meters (105 feet) thick in 2010 to 4 meters (13 feet) in 2023, Permana said. By November 2024, the ice at this site was gone. As the glaciers thin, they also break apart, and each new fragment adds exposed edges where ice can melt, compounding the losses. In the 2026 Landsat image, freshly uncovered bedrock appears between the remnants. Snow still falls in the area, but it doesn’t last long enough on the bare rock to build up into new ice. “It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has tracked Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite imagery. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.” To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts. Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows. “While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said. As for the remaining patches of ice, time will tell how long they last. Recent satellite studies suggest complete disappearance of the main glacial ice areas could occur around 2030. Permana noted that BMKG estimates suggest they could be gone much sooner, hastened by the current El Niño . Past El Niño years have hit these glaciers especially hard. As the air warms, the freezing level rises above the summit, so precipitation falls as rain instead of snow. That means less fresh white snow that normally reflects sunlight and shields the ice, leaving darker surfaces that absorb more heat and melt faster. During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than usual , losing roughly 5.3 meters (17 feet) of thickness in a single year. The 2023-2024 El Niño brought another bout of rapid thinning, about 2 to 4 meters (7 to 13 feet) per year. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition. These images were taken by the Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), a camera that is also located on the end of the rover’s robotic arm. Each hole has a diameter of 0.63 inches (16 millimeters). Curiosity was built by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. JPL leads the mission on behalf of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of NASA’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio. MAHLI was built by Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego. article.description: APOD Ciencia APOD APOD: 17 de noviembre de 2026 –… El APOD de hoy
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: APOD: 17 de noviembre de 2026 – Vía Láctea versus Aurora**

En la imagen del día de hoy, se presenta un fascinante contraste entre la Vía Láctea y una aurora boreal, capturada desde Kvaløya, Noruega. A la izquierda, la Vía Láctea se despliega como un arco central, representando un antiguo sistema de estrellas, gas y polvo que ha existido mucho antes de la formación de la Tierra. Este vasto conjunto de materia se encuentra a distancias inimaginables de nuestro planeta.

Por otro lado, a la derecha, se observa un arco auroral, un fenómeno que se forma en la atmósfera terrestre a partir de átomos y moléculas energizados. Este espectáculo natural es el resultado de partículas energéticas expulsadas por el Sol, que interactúan con el campo magnético de la Tierra. La imagen destaca cómo estos dos gigantes celestiales parecen competir por el dominio del cielo, aunque en realidad se encuentran en diferentes escalas y contextos temporales.

En el fondo de la imagen, se puede identificar la constelación del Gran Carro, y aún más lejos, la galaxia de Andrómeda, lo que añade una capa adicional de profundidad y maravilla a esta representación del cosmos.

article.original_title: APOD: 2026 November 17 – Milky Way versus Aurora
article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 17 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Original Annotated Milky Way versus Aurora Explanation: Are these two giant arches battling for control of the sky? No, but it sure looks like it! The arch on the left is the central band of our Milky Way Galaxy , an ancient system of stars, gas, and dust that predates our Earth and is very far away. The arch on the right, by contrast, is an auroral ribbon that is only hours old, composed of energized atoms and molecules , and is close by — right in Earth’s upper atmosphere . These chance-superposed titan s have our Sun in common, a stellar member of the Milky Way that ejects energetic particles which create aurora s. Far behind the middle of the auroral arch is the Big Dipper . Even farther in the distance is the Andromeda galaxy — the bright spot near the top of the frame, just left of center. The featured image was taken about a month ago from Kvaløya in northern Norway . article.description: La tercera isla más grande del mar Mediterráneo expone un trozo antiguo del fondo oceánico y alberga una colonia de gatos.
article.explanation:
**Chipre: Isla de serpientes, gatos y ofiolitas**

Chipre, una isla con una rica historia geológica, comenzó a formarse hace aproximadamente 90 millones de años. Este proceso se debió a la actividad volcánica en el fondo marino, que dio origen a una corteza oceánica que, con el tiempo, emergió gracias a fuerzas tectónicas. Las rocas ofiolitas, que caracterizan la isla, son visibles en las montañas Troodos.

El paisaje de Chipre ha sido moldeado por la sedimentación a lo largo de los años. Durante el Mioceno, se acumularon capas de rocas sedimentarias que contribuyeron a la formación de la península de Akrotiri, unida a la isla principal por dos tombolos. Esta península alberga el lago salado de Akrotiri, que, aunque históricamente ha atraído a grandes poblaciones de flamencos, ha visto una drástica disminución en su número, pasando de 4,000 aves a solo 30 en 2025.

Además, Chipre es famosa por su población de serpientes, especialmente las víboras de nariz plana. En el pasado, la isla fue conocida como Ophiousa, lo que refleja su abundancia de estos reptiles. Para controlar su población, se introdujeron gatos desde Egipto, y hoy en día, se estima que hay tantos gatos como habitantes en la isla, superando el millón.

article.original_title: Cyprus: Island of Snakes, Cats, and Ophiolites
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Cyprus: Island of Snakes,… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Seasonal rains had started to fill Akrotiri Salt Lake when the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 captured this image of Cyprus’s Akrotiri Peninsula on October 10, 2026. NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison The island of Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous , with molten rock pouring from the seafloor, solidifying, and building new oceanic crust . Over time, portions of this oceanic rock were wrenched upward by tectonic forces , eventually emerging as a rugged island made of ophiolite , a type of rock with a mottled green appearance said to look like the skin of a snake. Remnants of that ancient island are still visible in the dark rocks of the Troodos Mountains . During the Miocene , considerably younger layers of chalk, limestone, marl, and other marine sedimentary rocks accumulated around the island, providing material that developed into a second, smaller island to the south during a later period of geologic uplift . Over time, sediment poured from rivers into the channel separating the two islands and combined with marine sediments to create deltas and eventually two land bridges, or tombolos . The joined landmass comprises the Akrotiri Peninsula , now the southernmost tip of Cyprus. The sandy edges of the peninsula were visible when Landsat 8 captured these images on October 10, 2026. Akrotiri Salt Lake , a coastal lagoon that was once an arm of the Mediterranean Sea, lies between the two tombolos. The more westerly feature, the Kouris River tombolo, formed first, developing about 50,000 years ago from river-deposited gravels and sands. The eastern tombolo extended southward from Cyprus, cutting off the Mediterranean Sea only within the past 2,000 years, according to geologists . The lake’s water levels now vary markedly with the seasons, typically filling in the late autumn and winter and drying out in the summer. The influx of winter water has historically attracted sizable overwintering flamingo populations, averaging about 4,000 birds. However, the wintering flamingo population has declined in recent years, plummeting to 30 birds in 2025, according to news reports . Flamingos have long flocked to the lake to feed on fairy shrimp , which are rich in colorful substances called carotenoids that give the birds their famously pink hue . Snakes are another of the island’s more notorious animal inhabitants. In antiquity, Cyprus was known as Ophiousa , or “ land of snakes ,” likely due to its robust population of blunt-nosed vipers . According to legend, the island’s snake communities grew to be so problematic during a drought in the fourth century that the Roman Empress Helena , mother of Constantine the Great, called for shiploads of cats to be sent from Egypt to control the venomous reptiles. The first feline imports were released in a particularly snake-infested area on the southeastern part of the Akrotiri Peninsula, an area that came to be known as Cape Gata (Cape Cat in Greek). The cape today is still home to the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats , a place where legend says that monks encouraged newly arrived Egyptian cats to hunt snakes. Today, Cyprus has as many cats as people, with more than one million of the feline predators stalking the island. The handful of nuns who now live in the monastery still care for hundreds of cats, according to the St. Nicholas Center . A broader image of Cyprus captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 shows the western half of the island on October 10, 2026. Chipre: Isla de serpientes, gatos y ofiolitas Chipre, una isla con una rica historia geológica, comenzó a formarse hace aproximadamente 90 millones de años. Este proceso se debió a la actividad volcánica en el fondo marino, que dio origen a una corteza oceánica que, con el tiempo, emergió gracias a fuerzas tectónicas. Las rocas ofiolitas, que caracterizan la isla, son visibles en las montañas Troodos. El paisaje de Chipre ha sido moldeado por la sedimentación a lo largo de los años. Durante el Mioceno, se acumularon capas de rocas sedimentarias que contribuyeron a la formación de la península de Akrotiri, unida a la isla principal por dos tombolos. Esta península alberga el lago salado de Akrotiri, que, aunque históricamente ha atraído a grandes poblaciones de flamencos, ha visto una drástica disminución en su número, pasando de 4,000 aves a solo 30 en 2025. Además, Chipre es famosa por su población de serpientes, especialmente las víboras de nariz plana. En el pasado, la isla fue conocida como Ophiousa, lo que refleja su abundancia de estos reptiles. Para controlar su población, se introdujeron gatos desde Egipto, y hoy en día, se estima que hay tantos gatos como habitantes en la isla, superando el millón.

article.explanation:
**De contratista a funcionario público: La NASA le da la bienvenida a Jim Mirandy**

Jim Mirandy, especialista en aseguramiento de calidad en el Centro Espacial Stennis de la NASA, ha hecho la transición de contratista a funcionario público. Esta decisión forma parte de una directiva de la agencia para fortalecer las competencias técnicas dentro de su personal civil. Tras 30 años como contratista, Mirandy ahora desempeña un papel crucial en la misión de la NASA de devolver a los astronautas estadounidenses a la Luna a través del programa Artemis.

Mirandy ha sido fundamental en la implementación de protocolos de seguridad y en la formación de clases de entrenamiento en alta presión y criogénico. Su experiencia específica en el centro garantiza que las pruebas de propulsión se realicen con los más altos estándares de seguridad y calidad. Además, su trabajo incluye investigar incidentes y liderar programas de protección voluntaria.

Desde su infancia en Titusville, Florida, donde su padre trabajaba en la NASA, Mirandy ha estado vinculado al mundo espacial. Su trayectoria profesional comenzó en el Michoud Assembly Facility, donde su habilidad para resolver problemas lo llevó a enfocarse en la seguridad y la calidad. Su compromiso con la mejora continua y la seguridad de sus colegas es evidente en cada aspecto de su trabajo.

article.original_title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
article.source_body: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Jim Mirandy, quality assurance specialist at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, poses for a photograph at the High Pressure Gas Facility on Nov. 10, 2026. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce. NASA/Danny Nowlin The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA. “Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.” His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. They took the time to explain the test stands and other systems and how they worked.” A knack for fixing things helped launch Mirandy’s career at Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. He started working hands-on as a mechanic on the Space Shuttle External Tank. When an unexpected incident occurred in a production cell, Mirandy stepped up to help the operations and safety team resolve the issue. This moment shifted his career trajectory into safety and quality. Mirandy found his way to NASA Stennis and brought an understanding of systems and operations with him. A resident of Bay St. Louis and a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, Mirandy is motivated by helping people, keeping them safe, and improving processes. “Your reward for working safely today is tomorrow,” said Mirandy. article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Fotos de astronautas de Gemini inspiraron programa temprano de observación de la Tierra**

En noviembre de 1966, durante la misión Gemini XII, los astronautas James Lovell y Buzz Aldrin registraron imágenes del Mar Rojo y el valle del Nilo. Este último vuelo del programa Gemini no solo cumplió objetivos técnicos espaciales, sino que demostró el valor científico de observar la superficie terrestre desde la órbita.

Las fotografías capturadas por la tripulación fueron fundamentales para que científicos e instituciones justificaran la creación de un programa satelital dedicado. William T. Pecora, entonces director del Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos, fue un defensor clave de esta iniciativa tras notar la utilidad de los registros visuales obtenidos en las misiones Mercury y Gemini para el estudio de recursos
article.image_headline: Las fotos de Gemini XII impulsaron el desarrollo de satélites de observación terrestre, mejorando estudios ambientales.
article.original_title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
article.source_body: NASA astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. captured this image of the area surrounding the Red Sea and Nile river valley on November 14, 1966, during their four-day mission in space. Gemini XII was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini Program. NASA Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space. The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface. Their images helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program he championed, and which later paved the way for Landsat , was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.” For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet. article.explanation:
**NASA recibe decimosexta opinión de auditoría financiera "limpia" consecutiva**

NASA ha logrado, por décimo sexta vez consecutiva, una opinión de auditoría externa "limpia" sobre sus estados financieros del año fiscal 2026. Este reconocimiento, el más alto en auditoría, asegura que los informes financieros de la agencia cumplen con los Principios de Contabilidad Generalmente Aceptados para agencias federales y reflejan con precisión su situación financiera.

El administrador de NASA, Jared Isaacman, destacó la importancia de ser responsables en la gestión de los recursos públicos y subrayó que esta auditoría limpia es un testimonio del compromiso de la agencia con la rendición de cuentas financieras. El informe financiero de 2026 también resalta los avances en las misiones de NASA, incluyendo el exitoso vuelo de prueba de la misión Artemis II, que marcó hitos significativos en la exploración espacial.

Además, se anunciaron iniciativas transformadoras para fortalecer el liderazgo estadounidense en el espacio, como la construcción de una base lunar y el lanzamiento anticipado del telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman, destinado a estudiar fenómenos como la materia oscura y la energía oscura. Estos logros reflejan el compromiso de NASA con la transparencia y la innovación en la exploración espacial.
article.image_headline: NASA recibe decimosexta opinión de auditoría financiera "limpia" consecutiva
article.original_title: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion
article.source_body: Credit: NASA For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements. The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position. “Our responsibility at NASA is to be disciplined stewards of the resources entrusted to us by the American people while delivering on the missions they expect from this agency,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Our 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, and we intend to pair that discipline with the urgency and execution required to take on the near-impossible missions ahead.” The 2026 Agency Financial Report provides key financial and performance information and demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency in the use of American taxpayers’ dollars. In addition, the 2026 report presents progress during the past year, and spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development with these financial resources. In fiscal year 2026 (FY 2026), NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully accomplished a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, delivering major human spaceflight milestones, such as the record‑breaking distance astronauts have traveled from Earth and global public engagement. NASA also announced a series of transformative agencywide initiatives designed to advance American leadership in space, including plans to build a Moon Base, which will be humanity’s first lunar outpost, and a place where astronauts will live, work, and explore near the Moon’s South Pole. NASA’s science advancements in FY 2026 included launching the agency’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, ahead of schedule, to study dark matter, dark energy, planets outside our solar system, as well as exploration of everything from nearby stars to distant galaxies. NASA’s experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft achieved a major milestone when it flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time. The agency also: launched NASA Force with the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, a talent track designed to recruit and deploy the nation’s top engineers and technologists to support America’s space program; announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus; and welcomed additional Artemis Accords signatories committing to the safe, transparent, and responsible exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. article.description: Rondas de lluvias intensas en el suroeste de EE. UU. inundaron ríos y elevaron rápidamente el segundo embalse
article.explanation:
Entre fines de octubre y principios de noviembre de 2026, una serie de tormentas extremas azotó la región de Four Corners, en el suroeste de Estados Unidos. Este fenómeno, impulsado por temperaturas oceánicas inusualmente altas y el patrón de El Niño, provocó un aumento crítico en los caudales de la zona.

Según datos satelitales de la NASA, el Embalse Navajo, ubicado entre Nuevo México y Colorado, elevó su nivel en casi 18 metros en apenas siete semanas. Para el 7 de noviembre, el reservorio alcanzó el 108% de su capacidad promedio, su punto más alto desde agosto de 2019. Esto contrasta drásticamente con el 60% registrado en septiembre del mismo año.

Las consecuencias fueron duales. Por un lado, el desborde de ríos como el San Juan causó inundaciones severas en localidades como Pagosa Springs, obligando a evacuaciones y dañando infraestructura. Por otro lado, los expertos documentaron el fin de la sequía de corto plazo en el suroeste y la Gran Cuenca, aunque la escasez hídrica de largo plazo aún persiste en diversos sectores del territorio.

article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Water Surges Into Navajo… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Back-to-back extreme rain events inundated the Four Corners region of the U.S. Southwest in late October and early November 2026. The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods. One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir. The change is visible in the images above, acquired on September 20 (left) and November 7 (right) with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 . In that time, the lake in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado rose by nearly 60 feet (18 meters), according to data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. (Note that the Bureau of Reclamation decreased releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17.) On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date. That contrasts with September 20, when it held just 60 percent of its average capacity. Due to snow drought across the West in winter 2025-26, the lake saw relatively little growth in the spring, when snowmelt often raises water levels. The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers swelled with runoff amid the wet weather. Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town along the San Juan River about 40 miles (64 kilometers) northeast of the lake, was especially hard-hit by flooding. In the first round of rain, 5.05 inches (12.8 centimeters) fell in the town, and on October 23 the river reached major flood stage . After more rain, the river spiked again on November 1, this time nearly to the record level set in 1911 during a devastating flood . Officials issued evacuation orders, and responders rescued dozens of people, according to news reports , while water inundated streets and damaged property. Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks. From early September through early November, precipitation totals were 2 to 4 times the average throughout the Four Corners region—an area beset by long-term drought that was exacerbated by snow drought and high temperatures in 2026. Though the downpours posed hazards to communities along many rivers, they did provide drought relief throughout the region. Weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps, derived from a suite of satellite data products and ground-based observations, have indicated improvements to drought conditions due to the fall storms. The group’s November 3 summary noted that “short-term drought has ended for the Southwest and Great Basin,” although long-term drought persists in places. Wet weather in the Southwest is often associated with El Niño events, when the segment of the jet stream flowing eastward near the equatorial Pacific tends to strengthen. Experts noted that the low-pressure system delivering the heavy rainfall in autumn 2026 was at a low latitude for the time of year and drew energy from unusually high ocean temperatures. El Niño patterns—like the one currently underway —can increase the likelihood of moisture-laden storms being steered across the Southwest interior. article.explanation:
**El James Webb revela los secretos de la formación estelar en NGC 7129**

La NASA ha publicado una detallada imagen de la región de formación estelar NGC 7129, captada en luz infrarroja por el Telescopio Espacial James Webb. Esta tecnología permite atravesar el polvo opaco que usualmente bloquea la visión en luz convencional, revelando el complejo nacimiento de nuevos astros.

El proceso comienza cuando la gravedad agrupa masivas cantidades de gas. En la captura se distinguen dos zonas clave: a la izquierda, entre nubes de color dorado, se ubican estrellas jóvenes relativamente maduras. A la derecha, en la región rojiza, se encuentran astros en etapas más tempranas de su evolución.

La estructura filamentosa del gas rojo es consecuencia de los potentes chorros y vientos emitidos por las estrellas en formación. Estos fenómenos, que incluso pueden derivar en explosiones, moldean el entorno galáctico de manera dinámica.

El estudio de estas diferentes etapas

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb Explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light . Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds — and some then explode . Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image , with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right — in the red region. Jets and wind s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when. El James Webb revela los secretos de la formación estelar en NGC 7129 La NASA ha publicado una detallada imagen de la región de formación estelar NGC 7129, captada en luz infrarroja por el Telescopio Espacial James Webb. Esta tecnología permite atravesar el polvo opaco que usualmente bloquea la visión en luz convencional, revelando el complejo nacimiento de nuevos astros. El proceso comienza cuando la gravedad agrupa masivas cantidades de gas. En la captura se distinguen dos zonas clave: a la izquierda, entre nubes de color dorado, se ubican estrellas jóvenes relativamente maduras. A la derecha, en la región rojiza, se encuentran astros en etapas más tempranas de su evolución. La estructura filamentosa del gas rojo es consecuencia de los potentes chorros y vientos emitidos por las estrellas en formación.
